analysis.one_liner: Requires standardized nutrition labels on packaged food and sets rules for health claims.
analysis.headline: The bill died in House committee without a floor vote, but its subcommittee sent a rewritten version forward and a near-identical nutrition labeling law passed later the same Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every packaged food to carry a standard nutrition label listing serving size, calories, calories from fat, and amounts of fat, cholesterol, sodium, carbohydrates, sugars, protein, and fiber. It would also have stopped food companies from using terms like 'light' or 'low-fat' or making disease-related claims unless the food met government-defined standards. Enforcement would be shared with state governments.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers buying packaged food. Today, shoppers often cannot compare products because each company formats nutrition information differently, or omits it entirely. The bill would give every shopper the same standardized facts panel and would curb vague or misleading claims on the front of the package.

how_it_helps.text: Every packaged food must state serving size, servings per container, calories, calories from total and saturated fat, and amounts of total fat, saturated fat, unsaturated fat, cholesterol, sodium, total and complex carbohydrates, sugars, protein, and dietary fiber.

Terms like 'light' or 'low-fat' and disease-related claims can only be used if the Secretary of Health and Human Services defines them and the food actually contains amounts that reduce dietary risk, so labels would have to match the contents.
State governments could sue to enforce the new labeling rules in addition to federal enforcement, adding a second layer of oversight.
Raw produce would be exempt from package labels but sellers would still have to give shoppers the same nutrition information, so the requirement would not skip fresh food.

analysis.who_pays: Packaged food manufacturers, who would have to redesign labels within 18 months, test their products, and drop marketing claims their products cannot support. Food sold for immediate consumption at the place of sale, and food prepared in retail establishments, would be exempt from package labeling.

drawbacks.text: Compliance would impose real costs on food processors within 18 months of enactment, and smaller producers have less capacity than large ones to redesign packaging and reformulate products to keep their claims.
The bill exempts food sold for immediate consumption and food prepared in retail establishments from package labels, leaving restaurant and deli food out of the disclosure system.
The required nutrient list is fixed in statute; when nutrition science moves on, updating the panel would require another act of Congress rather than a routine regulation.
Allowing state-level enforcement of labeling rules creates two parallel systems of lawsuits that manufacturers would have to track.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is large and everyday: a single standardized facts panel on every packaged food, so shoppers can compare products and know that 'low-fat' or 'light' means something. The costs are real but modest and one-time for manufacturers, and the exemptions for restaurant and deli food are a genuine gap. On balance, the bill's design is straightforward and the burden falls on the industry that profits from the labels being unclear.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee after its subcommittee forwarded a rewritten bill in its place, and the full committee never acted before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Henry Waxman and eight other members introduced the bill on July 27, 1989, and it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee.
The Subcommittee on Health and the Environment held a hearing on the bill on August 3, 1989, before formal referral.
The subcommittee marked the bill up in October 1989 and on October 25 forwarded a clean replacement bill, H.R. 3562, to the full committee in lieu of H.R. 3028.
Neither H.R. 3028 nor any version of it received a vote in the full committee or on the House floor before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.
Comprehensive nutrition labeling did become law during that same Congress: a nutrition labeling and education act was enacted in late 1990, carrying the requirements this bill laid out.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Packaged food makers got extra months without mandatory standardized labels and health-claim rules, since no bill cleared the House in 1989, though the policy ultimately passed before the Congress ended.

for.name: Rep. Henry Waxman
for.role: House sponsor, chair of the Health and the Environment Subcommittee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and pushed it through his subcommittee's hearing and markup.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill or its replacement to the House floor; no full-committee vote appears in the record.

against.name: Food and beverage manufacturers
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandatory uniform nutrition labeling and restrictions on front-of-package health claims during the labeling debate.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan though lopsided: 22 of 25 cosponsors were Democrats and 3 were Republicans, and no recorded vote ever split the chambers.

industries.note: The bill would force every packaged product to carry a standardized nutrition panel and would strip marketing claims from products that do not meet defined thresholds. Its interest in flexible, self-designed labels and loose claim language runs against shoppers' interest in comparable, honest information.

Food sold for immediate consumption and food prepared in retail establishments would be exempt from package labeling, so the establishments selling that food would avoid the compliance costs their packaged-food competitors bear. The exemption leaves those calories unlisted for shoppers.

Raw agricultural commodities are exempt from package labels but sellers would still have to provide the same nutrition information in a form the Secretary prescribes, so the cost is lighter but not zero.

Claims about fat, cholesterol, sodium, or fiber, or about a food's relationship to disease, would only be allowed if the Secretary defines the terms and the product actually reduces dietary risk. Vague or unsupported claims would become illegal misbranding.
